items_missed: Agenda statement was strong on structure but missing two required pieces — he laid out the roadmap ('a few questions regarding the move and from there I'll be able to tell you what the hourly rate will look like') but said 'a few minutes' instead of the 10-15 minute timeframe, and never closed it with 'sound good?'. His only confirmation ask was 'is this a good time to talk to you about the move?', which is a permission check, not agenda confirmation
Never asked 'how are you today?' — opened with 'Sorry to bother', which is a self-diminishing frame on an outbound lead call he had every right to make
No zip codes captured on either address despite reading both addresses aloud

Never asked about additional stops — and this one bit him. Charles volunteered at the very end that 'there's a couple of things that are in there that I just need their help moving down to the dump.' Arden answered 'Okay, no problem' and then never mentioned it again, never asked where the dump is, never asked how many items, and never put a minute of it into the estimate
Never explicitly asked whether Charles wanted packing services — the box-count question surfaced 'I've already packed everything else' by luck rather than by asking
Storage was only probed as an origin room ('a storage unit within the building'), never as a storage stop on the route

Moving-stressor question replaced with a generic one — 'do you have any question any clarification regarding the moving process in general?' is not 'is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?', and it produced nothing

No day-of-week rate framing. The move is Friday September 4 and he quoted $222/hr flat with no mention that Monday-Thursday is the cheaper tier. On an outbound call to a lead who has not committed to a date, that is a real missed lever
No 'pricing is super simple' opener — he went from 'we're all good, sir' straight into the rate. He used 'very simple' later on the clock, not on pricing

Drive time never addressed as an estimate variable. Irving to Farmers Branch is a genuine loaded drive and the clock runs during it; he covered 'no transportation fee' but never told Charles the drive is billable time
Traffic never mentioned, on a 3:30 PM Friday arrival window in DFW. That is the single most predictable overage on this booking and it went unflagged

Estimate has two unpriced items baked into it — the dump run and carrying the bed frame up to the second floor — yet he told Charles 'I'm estimating the move to take only around two and a half to three hours' and described the destination as 'technically one story house since we're not going to be moving anything to the second floor.' Both statements were already contradicted by things Charles had said

Save Your Ass speech missing almost entirely. 'If the move goes faster than what we have expected... then of course you pay less' is estimate hedging, not the prep speech — no prep-equals-shorter-move-equals-lower-bill logic, no consolidation examples, no 'take a carload' tip, no close

Email handoff mentioned but never explained — no bolded detail list at the top, no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. On this call that verification ask was worth more than usual, because the unit number, the dump items and the bed frame all needed confirming in writing
Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' — 'if there's any question clarification prior to the move itself, you can just let us know' is an open door, not a check
Never gave business hours or a callback number
No 60 cents per pound baseline offered alongside the No Worries explanation, so the $2,000 coverage had nothing to be compared against

Delivery ran fast and script-heavy — 'no sterle fees', 'free evaluation coverage' (valuation), 'helping east tension of changes arriving at your front door', 'paraded in fifteen minutes', 'before I go over pricing structure and estimate thirty'. Charles's only responses across the entire pricing and clock block were 'Okay. Mm-hmm. Okay. Okay.'
top_strength: This is the strongest differentiator delivery in the batch and the discovery was disciplined. He ran a clean sequence — origin rooms, floor and elevator, truck parking, then measured both walk legs with the school bus equivalent and pushed back when the number was wrong ('It's probably like 23 school buses' / 'Oh, so there's gonna be a bit of a walk' / 'Just two school buses to be safe'), which is exactly the correction the equivalent tool exists to produce. He then hit four differentiator blocks in one confident run: the full what's-included list, the itemized no-hidden-fees pitch, No Worries with the mechanics spelled out ('up to $2,000... zero deductible... repaired, replace or reimburse for the fair market value'), Meet Your Mover, and the On-Time Guarantee. The clock section was perfect and closed properly with 'Does that all make sense, sir?', and the estimate was genuinely personalized — he narrated the fifth floor, the elevator, the walk, the zero boxes and the one-story unload back into the number before giving it.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, Arden: Charles handed you a scope change in the last minute of the call and you dropped it. 'There's a couple of things that I just need their help moving down to the dump' is a second stop, extra loading, extra drive time and possibly a dump fee, and your response was 'Okay, no problem. So we're all good, sir' — then you quoted 2.5 to 3 hours anyway. What you owed him was 'Let's make sure I've got that in the estimate — how many items, and is the dumpster on the property or are we driving somewhere? That's going to add about X, so let me adjust your range.' You did the same thing with the bed frame: he told you it goes upstairs, and minutes later you described his destination as 'technically one story house since we're not going to be moving anything to the second floor.' Your discovery is good — the problem is that late information never makes it back into the number, and that is precisely how a call that felt great turns into an over-estimate complaint on move day. Second priority: the Save Your Ass speech. You have never got a better setup for it than a customer with eight items and a dump pile — 'Charles, the biggest thing that keeps your bill down is prep. Anything small enough to fit in your car, take a carload over yourself. Get the loose stuff into drawers and boxes, get that dump pile stacked by the door so we're not hunting for it. The faster we can load, the shorter the clock runs. Does that make sense?' Third: slow down and put the customer back in the conversation. Charles said nothing but 'Okay' and 'Mm-hmm' for two straight minutes of your pricing block — break it into two pieces with a real check-in in the middle, and add the 10-15 minute timeframe plus a 'sound good?' to your opener, which is the only thing standing between your agenda statement and full credit.
phone_presence_notes: Courteous and well-organized — 'no problem', 'thank you for letting me know', 'congratulations Charles you're officially on the books' — but almost entirely one-directional: long scripted monologues with the customer reduced to monosyllables, acknowledgments recycled without variation ('Mm-hmm mm-hmm alright'), zero rapport or humor moments, and an apologetic 'Sorry to bother' open.
audio_review_reason: Section 9 clarity was scored 0 purely on transcript artifacts of fast, run-together script delivery ('no sterle fees', 'helping east tension of changes', 'free evaluation coverage'), and the customer went monosyllabic through the entire pricing and clock block. Audio is needed to tell whether he is genuinely rushing the script past the customer or whether the transcription is mangling normal-paced speech.
